strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and useful task formulation—transferring a full temporally-evolving effect from a reference video onto a separate input video/image (Ref + Input -> Output)—that is meaningfully different from prior static-reference or text-prompt-based editing paradigms.

Substantial engineering effort in constructing a large, diverse training corpus (>120K triplets, >1,700 effects) from three complementary sources (LoRA-based I2V, a novel automated V2V pipeline using first-last-frame interpolation + pose conditioning, and programmatic code-based effects), addressing the key bottleneck that video-to-video effect triplets do not naturally exist.

The proposed scalable V2V pipeline (image editing -> pose extraction -> conditional video generation) is a reasonable and creative solution to a genuinely hard data-generation problem, and could be of independent interest to the community.

Reasonably thorough evaluation combining qualitative comparisons, quantitative embedding-similarity metrics, VBench-style fidelity metrics, and a fairly large-scale human preference study (669/455/252 annotations across three settings) with consistent, large win-rate margins over baselines.

The classifier-free guidance decomposition enabling separate control over reference-effect adherence and input-video adherence (Sec 4.5) is a nice practical extension that increases the method's usability.
Honest discussion of limitations (occlusion handling, human-centric dataset bias, inference cost) rather than overselling results.
weaknesses: The 'tuning-free' framing in the title is somewhat inconsistent with the described training procedure, which fine-tunes a 14B parameter backbone with LoRA on a purpose-built dataset; the term appears to refer only to test-time behavior (no per-example optimization), but this could confuse readers and should be clarified up front.

No ablation studies isolating the contribution of each of the three dataset sources (LoRA I2V, custom V2V, code-based) to final model quality, nor ablations on architecture choices (e.g., width-wise vs channel-wise reference latent concatenation, mask design). This makes it hard to assess which components of the fairly complex data/model pipeline are actually necessary.

Much of the training data is itself synthetically generated by chaining several pretrained generative models (image generators, image editors, pose extractors, first-last-frame interpolators, GPT-4o for prompts), which risks compounding artifacts, distributional biases, and reduced fidelity to real-world effects; the paper does not analyze or quantify this risk (e.g., via manual quality audits beyond a brief filtering mention for V2V pairs).

Automatic quantitative metrics (VideoPrism/CLIP embedding similarity) are acknowledged by the authors themselves as only weakly correlated with actual task success, and the VBench-style fidelity metrics in the appendix show no clear differentiation between methods, leaving the human study as the only strong evidence of superiority—raising reproducibility/robustness concerns for future comparisons.

Validation sets are relatively small (56 I2V reference videos across 28 effects, ~100+ V2V pairs), which may limit the statistical reliability of the reported metrics and user-study conclusions given the diversity of effect types being claimed.
Code and dataset are not yet released (promised upon publication), limiting present reproducibility and independent verification of the dataset curation pipeline and claimed scale/diversity.

Baseline comparisons are inherently asymmetric (baselines only receive text prompts, since no other reference-conditioned baselines exist for this exact task), which is understandable given the paper's claim of introducing a new task, but it somewhat limits the strength of the 'outperforms baselines' claim since the comparison is more of an existence proof than a rigorous head-to-head against comparably-conditioned alternatives.

The paper's dataset is heavily skewed toward human-centric/foreground-dominant content (LoRA effects, Senorita human masks), which is acknowledged as a limitation but reduces the generality of the 'large-scale' and 'diverse' claims made in the abstract and contributions.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely underexplored problem: transferring a complex, time-varying visual effect from a reference video onto a separate target video/image, a setting distinct from prompt-based or keyframe-conditioned video editing.

Substantial engineering effort went into building a large triplet dataset from three complementary sources (LoRA-based I2V effects, a novel automated V2V pairing pipeline using image editing + pose-conditioned interpolation, and programmatic/code-based composited effects), yielding >120K triplets spanning >1,700 effects, which could be a useful resource if released.

The architecture extension (concatenating reference video latents width-wise alongside input video conditioning latents within an FLF2V backbone) is a clear, reasonably well-motivated way to jointly condition on reference and input signals, and the paper also demonstrates an interesting classifier-free guidance scheme for separately controlling adherence to input vs. reference.

Evaluation combines qualitative comparisons, embedding-based similarity metrics, and a sizeable human preference study (669/455/252 annotations across tasks), and shows consistent, large win-rates over strong baselines (Wan 2.1, Wan VACE variants, Lucy Edit) in reference adherence.

The paper is transparent about limitations (occlusion handling, human-centric data bias, 2x inference cost) and provides substantial supplementary detail on dataset construction, hyperparameters, and additional VBench-style quality metrics.
weaknesses: The core training data (especially the V2V triplets) is synthetically generated by chaining several other generative/editing models (Flux/Qwen image editors, Wan VACE, pose extractors, first-last-frame interpolation) rather than derived from real paired videos. This creates a risk that RefVFX is largely learning to imitate the stylistic biases and artifacts of this particular generation pipeline rather than a general notion of 'effect transfer,' and this circularity is not critically discussed.

There is no ground-truth validation set with real target videos; success is measured only via proxy embedding similarity (VideoPrism/CLIP) to the reference/input and subjective human preference. Embedding similarity to the reference is almost guaranteed to favor a model explicitly conditioned on that reference, making this metric only weakly informative of genuine effect-transfer quality versus simple copying/leakage of reference content.

Baselines are text-only (given paraphrased descriptions of the reference effect) and structurally cannot access the reference video at all, so the comparison mostly demonstrates the (unsurprising) benefit of having access to extra reference-video information rather than isolating the contribution of the proposed architecture or training recipe. No ablation compares against a reference-conditioned baseline trained on a subset of the same data or a simpler injection mechanism.

The VBench-style quality metrics (Table 10) show the method performs 'comparably' to baselines with no clear improvement in aesthetic score, motion smoothness, or dynamic degree, undermining claims of superior visual/temporal quality beyond reference adherence.

Despite citing Dynamic Concepts (LoRA-per-effect methods) as a related/competing approach, no direct quantitative or qualitative comparison against it is provided, leaving a gap in positioning against the closest prior art for temporally dynamic effect personalization.

The dataset's effect taxonomy leans heavily on stylized, often cartoonish LoRA transformations (e.g., 'turn into Mona Lisa,' 'add pizza cape') and human-centric foreground scenarios, raising questions about generalization to more subtle or professional VFX use-cases implied by the paper's framing (e.g., cinematic lighting, atmospheric effects).

Reproducibility is limited: the dataset relies on several closed/proprietary components (GPT-4o for prompt generation, various commercial-adjacent editing models), and code/data release is only promised ('upon publication'), with no immediate public artifact accompanying submission.

Qualitative results (main figures) appear curated/cherry-picked without systematic failure-rate reporting beyond the single limitation example in the supplement, making it hard to judge typical real-world robustness.

strengths: The paper tackles a novel and practically important problem: transferring temporally-varying visual effects from a reference video onto an arbitrary target video/image in a feed-forward manner, going beyond static-reference or text-only editing which cannot capture time-evolving phenomena.

The dataset construction pipeline is a substantial engineering contribution. It combines three complementary sources (LoRA-based I2V effects, an automated scalable V2V pipeline using first-last-frame interpolation + pose-conditioned regeneration, and programmatic code-based effects with temporal compositing) to produce >120K triplets spanning >1700 effects, addressing the core data-scarcity problem for this task in a scalable and reasonably well-justified way.

The architecture extension (frame-width-wise concatenation of reference video latents alongside channel-wise input video conditioning, with a hybrid mask) is a clean and sensible adaptation of the Wan FLF2V conditioning scheme to jointly encode reference effect and input video, and the paper provides a clear diagram (Fig. 5) of how this differs from the base model.

Evaluation is comprehensive relative to the difficulty of the task: qualitative comparisons across I2V and V2V settings, a fairly large human preference study (669/455/252 annotations across three settings) with consistent large win-rates and positive mean scores across many baselines, quantitative embedding-similarity metrics (VideoPrism/CLIP) showing the intended effect (higher reference similarity), and supplementary VBench-style fidelity metrics (aesthetics, motion smoothness, dynamic degree) showing no major quality degradation.

The controllable guidance mechanism (separate CFG directions for text, reference, and input video) is a nice practical addition that gives users interpretable control over the reference/input trade-off, and is demonstrated qualitatively.

The paper is transparent about limitations (occlusion handling, human-centric data bias, 2x inference cost) and provides very extensive supplementary detail on dataset construction (effect catalogs, hyperparameter tables), aiding reproducibility of the data pipeline even though the dataset itself may not be released alongside code.
weaknesses: Because no ground-truth triplets exist for the validation sets, the primary quantitative evidence is proxy similarity metrics (VideoPrism/CLIP) and a human study; the paper acknowledges these metrics "only partially reflect aesthetic and temporal nuances," and reference-similarity alone can be gamed by copying more of the reference content rather than truly fusing effect and input motion (the paper's own explanation that baselines have higher input-similarity due to "under-editing" cuts both ways for interpreting whether RefVFX's higher reference-similarity reflects better fusion or simply more reference leakage).

The human study, while sizable, is not fully described in the main text (annotator count, expertise, instructions, inter-rater agreement are deferred to supplement), making it harder to fully assess study rigor and potential bias from the paper's own team framing/selecting comparison videos.

No ablations are shown in the main paper isolating the individual contribution of each of the three dataset sources (LoRA I2V, custom V2V pipeline, code-based effects) to final model quality; given the dataset construction is a central contribution, an ablation on data source mixture would strengthen the claims of the pipeline's necessity/value.

The V2V data-generation pipeline chains many pretrained models (image gen, image editor x2, first-last-frame interpolation, pose extractor, conditional video generator), and it is unclear how much compounding artifacts/bias from this chain affect the final training data quality; only manual filtering is mentioned for the validation set, not systematically for training data.

The reported quantitative similarity gains are sometimes modest and inconsistent in direction (e.g., Table 3 Wan2.1 has higher first-frame similarity than RefVFX; Table 4 Wan VACE Depth has notably higher input similarity), and the paper does not provide statistical significance testing for the human study win-rates.

Effects tested for generalization (unseen LoRA effects, unseen code-based hyperparameters) are drawn from similar underlying families/distributions to training data; true out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., wholly different types of temporal phenomena, non-human-centric large-scale environmental effects) is only shown as a limitation case rather than evaluated systematically.

Code and full dataset release plans are stated as "upon publication" but not guaranteed within a firm scope (e.g., unclear if the LoRA-derived data, which relies on third-party assets, can be redistributed), which could limit reproducibility for external researchers wanting to rebuild the full training set.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated task: transferring dynamic, time-varying visual effects from a reference video onto a separate target video/image, which existing prompt-based or keyframe-based editing methods cannot address.

Proposes a genuinely scalable, multi-source data curation pipeline (LoRA-based I2V, an automated V2V pipeline using first-last-frame interpolation + pose conditioning, and programmatic code-based effects) that produces over 120K triplets spanning 1,700+ effects — a substantial engineering contribution that could be useful as a benchmark/dataset for future work.

The conditioning architecture extension of the Wan2.1 FLF2V backbone (width-wise latent concatenation of reference and input video tokens with a hybrid preservation mask) is clearly described and technically sound.

Comprehensive evaluation combining qualitative comparisons, a carefully designed large-scale human preference study (2AFC, practice trials, bootstrap confidence intervals, >15,000 annotations), and quantitative embedding-similarity and VBench-style metrics.
The multi-directional classifier-free guidance mechanism for controllable trade-off between input fidelity and effect adherence is a nice practical addition with qualitative demonstration.

Good transparency in limitations (occlusion handling, human-centric data bias, 2x inference cost) and detailed supplementary documentation of dataset/hyperparameters aiding reproducibility understanding.
weaknesses: Reported human-preference win rates are relatively modest (roughly 53-67%), especially for I2V (56.8-57.4% RVA) — the text's framing of these as "large preference"/"strong preference" is somewhat overstated relative to the actual margins.

No baseline exists that can accept a reference video as conditioning, so all comparisons are against text-only methods; this makes the comparison somewhat structurally favorable to RefVFX and leaves open whether the gains stem from the reference-conditioning idea specifically or simply from having strictly more information (reference video) than baselines with only text.

Lack of ground-truth triplets for validation forces reliance on embedding similarity as a proxy, and the quantitative story is mixed: baselines sometimes score higher on input similarity, which the paper interprets favorably as "under-editing" but could equally indicate the proposed method over-edits or leaks reference-specific content; no metric to check whether effect is content-independent (a core stated challenge in the method).

VBench-style quality metrics (Table 10, aesthetic score, motion smoothness, dynamic degree) are comparable across all methods, which somewhat weakens the argument that RefVFX offers a clear quantitative advantage beyond the (contested) similarity metrics.
No ablations isolating the contribution of each of the three data sources (LoRA I2V, custom V2V, code-based) to final model performance, despite this being a central claimed contribution.

The dataset construction pipeline depends heavily on several proprietary/closed models (Qwen-Image, Flux, GPT-4o, Wan2.1) for generating training pairs, which may hinder exact reproducibility even with code release.

"Tuning-free" in the title could be misleading, since the method requires large-scale supervised fine-tuning (LoRA on a 14B backbone) on a purpose-built dataset; the term is really only accurate with respect to test-time optimization, and this distinction is not clarified early enough.

strengths: Introduces a relatively novel and useful task formulation -- transferring a full temporally-evolving effect from a reference video onto an input image/video -- that is underexplored compared to prompt-based or static-reference editing.

Substantial engineering effort in constructing a large, diverse triplet dataset (>120K triplets, >1700 effects) from three complementary sources (LoRA-based I2V, a scalable V2V generation pipeline using chained image-edit + pose-conditioned video generation, and programmatic code-based effects), which could be a useful resource/benchmark for future work if released.

The architectural extension (width-wise concatenation of reference and input video latents with a hybrid preservation mask) is a sensible and relatively lightweight adaptation of an existing FLF2V backbone to the new conditioning setting.

Evaluation includes a reasonably large-scale human preference study (15K+ annotations, 500+ annotators) with bootstrap confidence intervals and a sensible 2AFC protocol (RVA/IVA/OM), along with qualitative comparisons across multiple baseline families (Wan2.1, VACE Pose/Depth, Lucy Edit).

Includes a controllable guidance mechanism (separate CFG terms for text/input/reference) enabling users to trade off adherence to input vs. reference, which is a nice practical feature with qualitative support.
Paper is transparent about limitations (occlusion handling, human-centric data bias, doubled inference cost) and provides substantial supplementary detail on dataset/effect taxonomies.
weaknesses: Quantitative win-rates in the user study are often modest (many in the 53-65% range with reported std of 2-5%), so several comparisons are only marginally above chance; the paper's framing of 'large preference' is not strongly supported by the numbers themselves.

No ablation studies isolating the contribution of each dataset source (LoRA I2V, custom V2V pipeline, code-based effects) or of key architectural choices (e.g., width-wise vs. channel-wise concatenation, the hybrid mask design), making it hard to assess which components actually drive performance.
The closest related finetuning-based method (Dynamic Concepts) is discussed in related work as directly relevant but is never empirically compared against, leaving an important baseline gap.

The automatic metrics used (VideoPrism/CLIP embedding similarity) are acknowledged by the authors themselves to only partially capture task success, and results are mixed/non-dominant across baselines (e.g., Wan VACE Depth sometimes scores higher on input similarity), undermining the quantitative evidence for the method's superiority.

The elaborate multi-stage data generation pipeline (chaining image generation, image editing, pose extraction, and conditional video generation models) likely introduces compounding artifacts and biases; quality control is described only briefly (manual filtering for one subset), with no systematic human quality assessment of the triplets themselves.
Dataset and code are not released at submission time ('upon publication'), limiting reproducibility verification during review despite the dataset being a central claimed contribution.

The method is explicitly content/human-centric in large portions of the training data (code-based effects filtered to human-centric masks), which the authors acknowledge limits generalization to broader environmental/cinematic effects -- a meaningful constraint on the claimed generality of the approach.

Limitations and failure analysis are illustrated with only a single qualitative example; a more systematic failure-mode analysis would strengthen the submission's credibility given the modest quantitative margins.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated task: reference-based video temporal effect transfer, distinguishing itself clearly from prompt-based or keyframe-conditioned editing methods that cannot capture time-varying effects.

Proposes a comprehensive and scalable data curation pipeline combining three complementary sources (LoRA-based I2V effects, a novel automated V2V pipeline using first-last frame interpolation + pose conditioning, and programmatic code-based effects), yielding a large-scale dataset (120K+ triplets, 1700+ effects) that could be a valuable resource for the community.

The V2V triplet generation pipeline (Fig. 4) is a creative and non-trivial technical contribution addressing a real data scarcity problem, since naturally-occurring reference/input/output video triplets do not exist.

Reasonable architectural design that extends the Wan2.1 FLF2V conditioning scheme to jointly incorporate reference effect video and input video via width-wise latent concatenation, with a sensible hybrid masking scheme.

Extensive evaluation combining qualitative results, quantitative embedding similarity metrics, and a large-scale human preference study (15,000+ annotations, 500+ annotators) with reasonable statistical treatment (bootstrap CIs).
Additional controllability analysis (dual classifier-free guidance over reference and input video) is a nice practical feature enabling user control at inference time.

The paper is transparent about limitations (occlusion handling, human-centric data bias, inference cost) and provides substantial supplementary detail (dataset composition, user study protocol, extended quantitative metrics).
weaknesses: The reported win rates in the human preference study are fairly modest (mostly 53-67%, often close to the 50% chance baseline, e.g., I2V RVA at 56.8-57.4%), which somewhat undercuts the claim of the method 'consistently' and 'largely' outperforming baselines; some deltas are within or near one standard deviation of chance.

Quantitative VBench-style metrics (Table 10, aesthetic/motion/dynamic degree) show the method is roughly comparable to or sometimes worse than baselines (e.g., lower dynamic degree in some settings), and this is not discussed critically in the main text.

No ablation studies isolating the contribution of each of the three dataset sources (LoRA I2V, custom V2V pipeline, code-based effects) to final model performance, making it hard to assess which data source drives most of the gains.

No ablation on the proposed conditioning/architecture design (e.g., alternative fusion mechanisms, effect of the hybrid mask, or removing width-wise reference concatenation) beyond the single 'No Ref' baseline, limiting insight into why the specific architectural choices were made.

The automated V2V data pipeline is complex and depends on multiple pretrained components (image generator, image editor, pose extractor, conditional video generator); potential compounding of errors/artifacts across this pipeline and their downstream impact on training data quality is not quantitatively analyzed.

Reliance on VideoPrism/CLIP embedding similarity as the primary quantitative proxy for effect transfer quality is acknowledged as imperfect by the authors themselves, but no additional automatic metric (e.g., an effect-specific classifier or a video-language model-based judge) is used to corroborate results beyond human study.

The paper does not report evaluation on truly out-of-distribution effect categories beyond 'unseen' variants of similar effect types already represented in the training taxonomy (human-centric, stylistic transformations, weather effects), so generalization claims to genuinely novel effect classes are not strongly substantiated.
Code and full dataset release is only promised ('will be released upon publication'), so reproducibility currently cannot be independently verified by reviewers.

The paper title/abstract claims 'tuning-free' but the method requires substantial LoRA fine-tuning of a 14B parameter backbone for 10K steps, which is a training-time cost; the 'tuning-free' framing refers only to inference-time behavior and could be clarified to avoid confusion with typical zero-shot 'tuning-free' methods in prior literature.
